children.text: Windows doesn’t expose everything. This page lists, route by route and signal by signal, what Intercept can prove and where the line is, so you never have to guess.
input routes can be paused, in the apps you choose
routes are reported as not paused, never hidden
between hook renewals, with gaps recorded

Software can reach an app in many ways. Intercept pauses only the route Windows flags as injected keyboard and mouse input. The others are reported as not paused, and are never folded into a “protected” claim.
Covered in the apps you choose, until you resume
A separate pointer control with native delivery tests
Control at the device or session source
Cooperation from the automation client or the app
A browser integration that pauses known clients
Secure desktop · another user · a VM
A verified control in each environment
An explicit adapter, tested before any claim
For virtual input devices, Intercept classifies the device transport and counts virtual-keyboard events. That is detection, not blocking.
Blocked counts are guard decisions, not proof of delivery.
A receipt shows the guard asked for an event to be stopped. It doesn’t measure what the recipient finally received.
Which app used the sensor, and when, from Windows’ own records
Which process connected where, with traffic per hour
Encrypted contents. Very short connections can be missed; names from DNS are marked as inferred
Every child process traced to the signed agent that started it
Activity inside WSL, which is attributed to WSL, not itemised
Input passes only into approved apps during a signature-verified session
Whether another program typed into the same app during that session
Names, ages and permissions of saved sign-ins and extensions
Passwords, cookie values or token contents. They are never read
Same-user termination. Any program running as you can end a standard-user guard. The watchdog relaunches it within 2 s and records the gap with its cause.
Elevated windows. A standard-user guard can’t act on input aimed at elevated windows. The optional elevated guard, still in development, addresses this.
Hook renewal. Hooks are replaced every 30 seconds. Windows can remove a timed-out hook silently between renewals.
Earlier hooks. Another program’s hook earlier in the chain can handle an event before Intercept’s guard sees it.
An allowance lets a trusted agent’s input through to an approved app during its session. Intercept always shows how strong the evidence was.
The recipient and a narrow time window only
Also matched an input marker found during calibration
A Windows trace names the agent’s helper process
Allowances never apply to protected apps. When markers exist, a mismatch blocks the event and raises a medium finding. Without an active, calibrated session, an agent gets no allowance at all.
